sections.b: John opens his Gospel by calling Jesus "the Word" (logos): "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). The phrase gathers the Bible's picture of God creating by speaking (Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6), Jewish Wisdom who was with God at creation (Proverbs 8:22–31), and the Logos of Greek and Jewish philosophy (Philo). What is new is the claim of John 1:14: the Word "became flesh and pitched his tent among us". The Word is not only God's message but God's self-expression in a human life.
sections.refs: John 1:1–18; Genesis 1:1–3; Proverbs 8:22–31; Sirach 24:8; 1 John 1:1; Revelation 19:13

common: In John 1 "the Word" is a title for the Son of God before he was born as Jesus.
uncommon: Some scholars (Boyarin) read John's Word as a Jewish idea of God's Memra or Logos, shared with the Targums and Philo, not a Greek borrowing.

sections.b: John uses "only Son" (monogenēs) of Jesus four times (John 1:14, 18; 3:16, 18). The word means "one of a kind", not "begotten" in a technical sense, though Latin "only-begotten" shaped later creeds. At John 1:18 the oldest manuscripts call Jesus "only God" rather than "only Son". Nathanael's confession, "you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel!" (John 1:49), uses the title in its royal sense, the king God adopts as son (Psalm 2:7), but the Gospel fills it with more: the Son shares the Father's life and work.
sections.refs: John 1:14; John 1:18; John 1:34; John 1:49; John 3:16–18; John 3:35–36; Psalm 2:7

common: "Only Son" in John stresses that Jesus is God's Son in a unique way, unlike believers who become God's children.

sections.b: John the Baptist points to Jesus twice as "the Lamb of God" (John 1:29, 36), and the first time adds, "the one who takes the world's sin away". No earlier text uses the phrase. Readers hear in it the Passover lamb (John dates Jesus' death to the day the lambs were slaughtered, John 19:14, 36), the servant of Isaiah 53 who goes "like a lamb that is taken off to slaughter" (Isaiah 53:7) and bears others' sins, the daily lambs of the temple, and the ram God provided in Isaac's place (Genesis 22:8). C. H. Dodd suggested that the Baptist meant a warrior lamb of judgment, like the Lamb in Revelation.
sections.refs: John 1:29; John 1:36; John 19:14; John 19:36; Exodus 12:3–13; Isaiah 53:7; Genesis 22:8; Revelation 5:6

sections.b: The Fourth Gospel never calls him "the Baptist" and never tells of Jesus being baptized by him. Its John is above all a witness: "This man came for testimony" (John 1:7). He denies being the Messiah, Elijah or the Prophet (John 1:20–21), calls himself only a voice from Isaiah 40:3, and points his own disciples to Jesus (John 1:35–37). His last words sum up his role: "He must keep growing, and I must keep getting smaller" (John 3:30). The Gospel also preserves the memory that Jesus' first disciples came from John's circle and that for a time both men baptized side by side (John 3:22–24).

uncommon: Some scholars think the Gospel stresses John's lower rank because it was answering a group that honored John as the Messiah.

sections.b: In John the temple action comes at the start of Jesus' ministry (John 2:13–22), not at the end as in the other Gospels. When asked for a sign, Jesus says, "Tear this temple down, and within three days I will raise it" (John 2:19), and John explains that he meant his body. The Gospel builds on this: the Word "pitched his tent among us" (John 1:14), worship will be neither on Gerizim nor in Jerusalem (John 4:21), and the festivals of the temple find their meaning in him. For readers after AD 70, when the temple lay in ruins, this said that God's dwelling with his people had not ended.

claude.title: Claude's theory: the temple scene as a headline
claude.body: John may have put the temple scene first the way a newspaper puts its main story on page one: not to change the date, but to tell readers how to read everything that follows, as the story of a new temple raised on the third day.

sections.b: John 4 is the longest meeting between Jesus and a Samaritan in the Gospels. At Jacob's well near Sychar, under Mount Gerizim, a Samaritan woman is surprised that a Jew would ask her for a drink, "For Jews do not share vessels with Samaritans" (John 4:9). She raises the dispute over the holy mountain, and Jesus says both Gerizim and Jerusalem will give way to worship "in spirit and truth" (John 4:23). Her town comes to believe and calls Jesus "the Savior of the world" (John 4:42). In John 8:48 Jesus' opponents insult him as a Samaritan.
sections.refs: John 4:4–42; John 8:48; Genesis 33:18–20; Deuteronomy 27:4–12; 2 Kings 17:24–41; Acts 8:4–25

common: Jews and Samaritans in Jesus' day shared the Torah but bitterly disputed where God should be worshiped.
uncommon: Some scholars read the woman's five husbands as a symbol of the five peoples whose gods were brought into Samaria (2 Kings 17:24–31).

sections.b: John says Jesus' way "had to take him through Samaria" (John 4:4). This was the quickest road between Judea and Galilee, though some pilgrims avoided it. He stops at Sychar, near ancient Shechem, beside the land Jacob gave Joseph (Genesis 48:22; Joshua 24:32). Many in the town believe (John 4:39–42), the first group of non-Judeans to believe in John's Gospel.

Jesus tells Nicodemus that "unless someone is born from above, he has no way to see the kingdom of God" (John 3:3). The Greek anōthen means both "from above" and "again", and Nicodemus hears only the second. Jesus explains the birth as "from water and Spirit" (John 3:5), as invisible and free as the wind (John 3:8). John 1:12–13 has already said that believers are born "of God", not of human descent or will. Churches have read this new birth as given in baptism, as a conscious conversion, or as both.
sections.refs: John 1:12–13; John 3:3–8; Ezekiel 36:25–27; Titus 3:5; 1 Peter 1:3; 1 Peter 1:23; 1 John 3:9

common: The new birth is God's work, not something people achieve.
uncommon: Some scholars read "water" in John 3:5 as natural birth (the water of the womb), followed by birth from the Spirit.

sections.b: John's Gospel does not narrate Jesus' baptism, but it is full of water and washing. John the Baptist baptizes "in water" so that Jesus may be revealed, and says Jesus will baptize "in the Holy Spirit" (John 1:31–33). Jesus' disciples baptize while John is still baptizing (John 3:22–23; 4:1–2). "Born from water and Spirit" (John 3:5) became the church's main text on baptism as new birth; Reformed and Baptist readers often take the water as a picture of the Spirit's cleansing (Ezekiel 36:25–27).
sections.refs: John 1:26–33; John 3:5; John 3:22–26; John 4:1–2; Ezekiel 36:25–27; Acts 2:38

sections.b: Jesus' first sign is turning water in six stone jars, kept for purity washings, into something like 120 to 180 gallons of fine wine at a village wedding (John 2:1–11). The man running the feast says the good wine was kept "until now" (John 2:10). The prophets had pictured God's coming age as a time of abundant wine (Amos 9:13–14; Isaiah 25:6), and Jesus elsewhere compares himself to a groom whose guests do not fast (Mark 2:19–22). Many Christians also see a link to the wine of the Lord's Supper.
sections.refs: John 2:1–11; Amos 9:13–14; Isaiah 25:6; Mark 2:19–22; Genesis 49:11

sections.b: John never names Jesus' mother. She appears at Cana at the beginning of the signs (John 2:1–12) and at the cross (John 19:25–27), and both times Jesus calls her "Woman". At Cana she tells him the wine is gone; he answers, "What does that have to do with me and you, woman? My hour is not here yet" (John 2:4), yet she tells the servants, "Whatever he says to you, do it" (John 2:5). Catholic and Orthodox Christians see her intercession here; most Protestants stress Jesus' independence from family claims and Mary's example of trust.

John the Baptist describes himself as the groom's friend who rejoices to hear the groom's voice (John 3:29), echoing the prophets who called God Israel's husband (Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20). The Gospel frames Jesus' early ministry with wedding imagery: a wedding at Cana (John 2:1–11), the groom and his friend (John 3:29), and a meeting at a well (John 4:5–26), the setting where Isaac, Jacob and Moses found their wives.
sections.refs: John 2:1–11; John 3:29; John 4:5–26; Genesis 29:1–12; Exodus 2:15–21; Isaiah 62:5; Revelation 21:2

sections.h: Heaven open over the Son of Man (John 1:51)
sections.b: Jesus promises Nathanael, "you will see heaven standing open, and God's angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man" (John 1:51). The words echo Jacob's dream at Bethel, where angels went up and down a stairway (Genesis 28:12). A Jewish reading in Genesis Rabbah 68:12 notes that the Hebrew can mean the angels went up and down "on him", that is, on Jacob himself. Jesus puts the Son of Man in that place: he is the meeting point between heaven and earth. Nathanael, "a real Israelite, with no trickery in him" (John 1:47), is the opposite of Jacob the trickster.
sections.refs: John 1:47–51; Genesis 27:35–36; Genesis 28:10–17; Genesis 32:28

uncommon: Some scholars think John 1:51 makes Jesus the new Bethel, "house of God", in line with John's temple theme.

sections.h: The snake and the Son of Man (John 3:14)
sections.b: Jesus tells Nicodemus that "As Moses raised the snake high in the wilderness, so the Son of Man has to be lifted up, so that each one who believes may have eternal life in him" (John 3:14–15). In Numbers 21:8–9 bitten Israelites who looked at the bronze snake on a pole lived. Jewish interpreters stressed that the snake had no power of its own (Wisdom of Solomon 16:6–7; Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:8); healing came from God as people turned to him. In John the pole becomes the cross, where Jesus is both raised up and exalted.
sections.refs: Numbers 21:4–9; 2 Kings 18:4; Wisdom of Solomon 16:5–7; John 3:14–15; John 8:28; John 12:32–34

sections.b: The phrase that fills Matthew, Mark and Luke appears in John only twice, both in the talk with Nicodemus: no one can see or enter the kingdom of God without being born from above (John 3:3, 5). Elsewhere John speaks instead of "eternal life", the life of the age to come that begins now (John 3:15–16, 36). Many scholars think John restated Jesus' kingdom message in terms of life for readers outside Palestine.
sections.refs: John 3:3; John 3:5; John 3:15–16; John 18:36; Mark 1:15; Mark 10:15

sections.b: In John's early chapters the Spirit comes down on Jesus "like a dove" and stays on him (John 1:32–33), so that he will baptize in the Holy Spirit. The Spirit gives the new birth, blowing like the wind where it wants to (John 3:5–8), and God "does not give the Spirit by measure" (John 3:34). True worshipers worship "in spirit and truth", because "God is spirit" (John 4:23–24). Jesus' "living water" (John 4:10) is later explained as the Spirit (John 7:39).

John 1 shows the range of first-century hopes. The Jerusalem delegation asks John the Baptist whether he is the Messiah, Elijah or "the Prophet" (John 1:19–25), three distinct figures. Andrew announces, "We have found the Messiah!" (John 1:41), and John translates the Hebrew title for Greek readers. In John 4 a Samaritan woman expects a Messiah who "will announce all things to us" (John 4:25), closer to the Samaritan Taheb, a prophet like Moses, than to a son of David. Only to her does Jesus say plainly, "I am he" (John 4:26).
sections.refs: John 1:19–25; John 1:41; John 1:45; John 4:25–29; Deuteronomy 18:15–18; Malachi 4:5

sections.b: In John's first chapters "the Jews" usually means the Jerusalem authorities, who send priests and Levites to question John (John 1:19) and challenge Jesus in the temple (John 2:18–20). The phrase also marks customs ("the Jews' purification rites", John 2:6; "the Jews' Passover", John 2:13), explained for non-Jewish readers. Jesus himself is "a Jew" to the Samaritan woman (John 4:9), and tells her that "salvation comes from the Jews" (John 4:22). These chapters are a reminder that the Gospel's sharp language later is a quarrel within Israel's family, not a rejection of Jews as such.
sections.refs: John 1:19; John 2:6; John 2:13; John 2:18–20; John 3:1; John 4:9; John 4:22

common: In many passages "the Jews" in John means the Judean leaders, not every Jewish person.

sections.b: The delegation to John the Baptist asks if he is "the Prophet" (John 1:21, 25), the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15–18. Philip tells Nathanael they have found the one "Moses wrote about" (John 1:45). The Samaritan woman, whose people looked for a returning prophet like Moses, calls Jesus "a prophet" (John 4:19) and then wonders if he is the Messiah (John 4:29).
sections.refs: John 1:21; John 1:25; John 1:45; John 4:19; John 4:25; Deuteronomy 18:15–18; John 6:14; John 7:40

sections.b: The first four chapters set out the Gospel's method. A prologue tells readers who Jesus is (John 1:1–18). Witnesses lead others to him (John 1:19–51). Signs reveal his glory (John 2:11; 4:54). Conversations turn on misunderstandings, with Nicodemus and the Samaritan woman as a deliberate pair: a leader of Israel who comes at night, and an unnamed Samaritan woman met at noon. The section runs from Cana to Cana (John 2:1; 4:46) and moves from Jews to Samaritans to a royal official, showing faith spreading outward.

The Samaritan woman asks where God should be worshiped, on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem (John 4:20). Jesus answers that the hour is coming when the place will no longer matter: "real worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth" (John 4:23), because "God is spirit" (John 4:24). Most interpreters read "spirit" as God's Spirit and "truth" as the reality revealed in Jesus. Some Christian groups, notably the Quakers, have read the verse as a call to worship without set forms.
sections.refs: John 4:19–24; John 2:19–21; Romans 12:1; Philippians 3:3

sections.b: Jesus tells his disciples, "raise your eyes and take in the fields. They are white for harvest" (John 4:35), as the Samaritans come out of the town. Ordinarily four months separate sowing from harvest; here sowing and reaping happen together, as Amos 9:13 imagined for the days of renewal. The proverb "One person sows, and someone else harvests" (John 4:37) becomes good news: the disciples reap where others worked.
sections.refs: John 4:35–38; Amos 9:13; Matthew 9:37–38; Luke 10:2; 1 Corinthians 3:6–9

sections.b: John 3:16 is the center of a long debate over whom Christ died for. Arminian, Wesleyan, Catholic and Lutheran readers see in "the world" every person, and in "everyone who believes" an open invitation. Reformed readers often understand "world" as humanity in its rebellion, or all kinds of people, and hold that God's saving purpose secures the elect. John's Gospel holds side by side God's love for the world (John 3:16–17) and the Father's drawing and giving of people to the Son (John 6:37, 44).
